site.name: Canadian Forum Against Organized Crime
site.tagline: Securing the Gateways and Borders Coast-to-Coast
site.description: A free one-day symposium on organized crime at Canada's ports, airports and land borders, for police, border and transport partners, prosecutors, corrections, analysts and community partners. Three cities, coast to coast.

content.aboutLead: Organized crime does not stop at a provincial line. It moves through the gateways the country depends on: container terminals, airports, rail yards, land crossings and the highway corridors between them.
aboutBody: The Canadian Forum Against Organized Crime is a one-day national symposium. It puts the people who work those gateways in the same room: police, border services and transport partners, port and airport authorities, prosecutors, corrections and probation staff, intelligence analysts, and the community organizations that see the downstream harm first.

The programme is built around current, practical material: how criminal networks exploit Canadian entry points, and what enforcement and disruption look like now. Information sharing runs through the whole day, including where it breaks down between agencies and jurisdictions and what has worked to fix that. Sessions are pitched at people who will take the material back to their own caseloads.

The Forum runs in three cities. Each is a standalone one-day event, free to attend, with a regional view of the same national problem. Victoria is confirmed. The Central Canada and Atlantic Canada events are being planned, and both are announced on this site once the city and date are set.
content.themesIntro: Themes are drawn from the ground the Forum has covered before. Sessions are confirmed closer to each event, and not every theme runs in every city.

themes.title: Contraband tobacco and nicotine products
themes.body: Illicit trade in tobacco and the wider range of nicotine products, and how regulatory decisions shape the market that enforcement then has to police.

themes.title: Online illicit sales
themes.body: How illicit goods move through websites, marketplaces and social platforms, and what has worked to disrupt the sellers behind them.

themes.title: Interdiction on the open web
themes.body: Targeting websites, marketplaces and social media accounts — the civil and regulatory levers that sit alongside criminal enforcement.

themes.title: Online monitoring and intelligence
themes.body: Running an online monitoring programme: current trends, what analysts are seeing, and where the work gets difficult.

themes.title: Industry and law enforcement working together
themes.body: What private-sector investigators, brand protection teams and regulators bring to a case, and how those partnerships are set up.

themes.title: Gang trends and migration patterns
themes.body: How groups are moving between regions, what the current indices show, and what that means for the receiving community.

themes.title: Gangs and human trafficking
themes.body: The links between gang activity and trafficking, indicators frontline staff can act on, and what a survivor-centred response asks of each agency.

themes.title: Social media and gang violence
themes.body: The role online platforms play in recruitment, in escalating disputes, and in the evidence that follows.

themes.title: Community reporting and Crime Stoppers
themes.body: Anonymous reporting as a public safety tool, and what it contributes to community safety and to investigations.

themes.title: Public health and public safety
themes.body: Where enforcement activity meets public health outcomes, and how the two sectors can work together rather than past each other.

themes.title: Gateways, ports and border crossings
themes.body: The regional entry points that let contraband, product and people move — and what interdiction looks like at each.

themes.title: Proceeds of crime
themes.body: Following the money behind illicit trade, and the financial trail that connects organized groups across jurisdictions.

faq.q: How much does it cost to attend?
faq.a: Nothing. Every event in the series is free, and lunch and refreshments are included. Travel and accommodation are at your own expense.
Registration runs on ONGIA's own events site. Use the Register button for the city you want to attend. Places are limited and allocated in the order they are received, so register early.

faq.q: Can I attend more than one city?
faq.a: Yes. Each event is registered separately. The themes are shared; the regional content differs.

faq.q: Do I need to be a police officer to attend?
faq.a: No. The Forum is open to everyone listed under Who should attend. Some sessions may be restricted to law enforcement. Where that applies, it is marked in the final programme.

faq.q: Will sessions be recorded or streamed?
faq.a: No. The Forum is in person only. Sessions are not streamed and recording is not planned, so presenters can speak frankly.

faq.q: Is there a certificate of attendance?
faq.a: Tell us when you register if you need a certificate of attendance or a record of professional development hours, and we will confirm what we can provide for that event.

Tell us about accessibility or dietary requirements when you register and we will arrange what we can with the venue. If you have a specific question about the building, the rooms or getting around the site, write to us before you register and we will get an answer from the hotel.
Contact the organizers in advance. Some sessions may be closed to media, and access is arranged case by case.

faq.q: Can my organization sponsor or exhibit?
faq.a: Write to the organizers and we will tell you what is available for that city.
